name: Amoz
title: The father of the prophet Isaiah
summary: Amoz is exclusively known as the father of the great prophet Isaiah, and his name appears consistently in the formula "Isaiah, son of Amoz" throughout the Hebrew Bible—at least 13 times. Although Scripture gives no direct information about his own life or work, the consistent use of this patronymic suggests that Amoz was a person of standing in the kingdom of Judah. Rabbinic tradition links him to the royal house by claiming he was the brother of King Amaziah, which would have made Isaiah part of the Davidic lineage. Amoz lived in turbulent times when the small states of the Levant were under increasing pressure from the Neo-Assyrian Empire, and this geopolitical reality formed the backdrop for his son's prophetic calling. His name (Hebrew: אָמוֹץ) means "strong" and is linguistically entirely distinct from the prophet Amos (עָמוֹס), although the names can be confused in Norwegian rendering.

keyEvents.title: Mentioned as Isaiah's father in the book's introduction
keyEvents.description: Amoz is identified as the father of the prophet Isaiah in the opening verse of the Book of Isaiah, where Isaiah's visions are dated to the reigns of kings Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah of Judah.

keyEvents.title: Isaiah sent to King Ahaz
keyEvents.description: During the Syro-Ephraimite War, Isaiah was sent with a message to King Ahaz, where he is identified as 'Isaiah son of Amoz,' emphasizing the prophet's lineage and authority in his encounter with the king.

keyEvents.title: Isaiah's message to Hezekiah concerning Assyria
keyEvents.description: When the Assyrian king Sennacherib threatened Jerusalem, Isaiah—identified as 'son of Amoz'—sent a message to King Hezekiah promising God's protection and judgment against Assyria.

keyEvents.title: Mentioned in 2 Kings
keyEvents.description: In 2 Kings, Amoz is identified as the father of the prophet Isaiah in connection with Isaiah's role as an advisor during King Hezekiah's reign, notably regarding Sennacherib's threat and Hezekiah's illness.

keyEvents.title: Mentioned in 2 Chronicles
keyEvents.description: 2 Chronicles refers to "the prophet Isaiah, son of Amoz" in connection with records about King Uzziah's deeds and King Hezekiah's reign, where Isaiah and Hezekiah pray together to the Lord during Sennacherib's threat.

versions.title: The father of the prophet Isaiah
versions.reason: [minor] The role 'patriarch' is somewhat misleading for Amoz. He is not a patriarch in the biblical sense (like Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob). A more fitting role would be 'father of the prophet Isaiah' or simply 'father'. Since we know very little about him, the role should reflect what we actually know.; [major] Isaiah 37:21 does indeed mention 'Isaiah, son of Amoz', but this event parallels 2 Kings 19:20. The verse is correct, yet the description 'Prophecy against Assyria' is somewhat imprecise—it concerns more specifically Isaiah's message to King Hezekiah regarding Sennacherib and Assyria's threat.; [major] The profile completely lacks footnotes. There are interesting linguistic, rabbinic, and historical details about Amoz that should be included, such as the difference between Amoz (אָמוֹץ) and the prophet Amos (עָמוֹס), as well as the rabbinic tradition concerning his connection to the royal house.; [minor] The summary is good but could clarify that the Jewish tradition stating Amoz was the brother of King Amaziah originates from the Talmud (Megillah 10b)—without mentioning this explicitly, it can be strengthened by saying 'according to rabbinic tradition'.; [minor] In Isaiah 6:1, Amoz is not actually named in the call vision itself across all textual traditions as clearly. It is more precise to say that the verse refers to 'Isaiah's vision' in the year King Uzziah died—but Amoz's name does not actually appear in Isaiah 6:1 in the base text. Amoz is mentioned in Isaiah 1:1, but in Isaiah 6:1 it simply says 'In the year that King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord...'. This event should be removed or corrected.

footnotes.text: The name Amoz (Hebrew: אָמוֹץ, ʾĀmōṣ) is derived from the root א-מ-ץ meaning "to be strong". It must not be confused with the prophet Amos (Hebrew: עָמוֹס, ʿĀmōs), which is derived from a different root (ע-מ-ס, "to bear"). The two names have different consonants in Hebrew and are completely distinct.

According to rabbinic tradition transmitted in the Babylonian Talmud (Megillah 10b), Amoz was the brother of King Amaziah of Judah. This tradition is based partly on the principle that when a prophet's father is named by name in Scripture, the father was also a prophet or a person of significance. If this is correct, Isaiah would have belonged to the royal Davidic lineage.

Amoz lived in an era when the Neo-Assyrian Empire dominated the Middle East. Under rulers such as Tiglath-Pileser III (745–727 BC), Sargon II (722–705 BC) and Sennacherib (705–681 BC), the small states of the Levant were subjected to military pressure, tribute demands and deportations — the direct historical context for his son Isaiah's prophetic activity.

Amoz is mentioned at least 13 times in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in the formula "Isaiah, son of Amoz". This consistent identification is unusual and may indicate that Amoz was a well-known figure, possibly with ties to the court in Jerusalem or to a prominent family in Judah.

The fact that Isaiah is consistently identified by the patronymic "son of Amoz" may also have had a rhetorical function: it established the prophet's legitimacy and authority before the kings he addressed, especially in politically charged situations such as the Syro-Ephraimite War and Sennacherib's siege of Jerusalem.

Archaeological finds from Jerusalem, including bullae (clay seals) from the 8th century BC, have confirmed the existence of several people mentioned in connection with Isaiah's work. Although no bulla with Amoz's name has been found, these finds illustrate that the court environment in Jerusalem was well documented and that patronymic identification was standard practice in official contexts.
